Galois theory. It connects the structure of polynomial equations to the symmetries of their solutions through group theory. Évariste Galois proved that a polynomial equation is solvable by radicals, meaning nth roots, if and only if its Galois group is solvable. This theory answers the ancient question: why does the quintic, the degree-five polynomial, have no general closed-form solution? Galois theory stands as one of mathematics' most elegant unifications, revealing why algebra and symmetry are inseparable.

The Galois group of a polynomial is the group of permutations of its roots that preserve rational operations. More formally, it consists of automorphisms of the splitting field that fix the base field. For a quadratic a x squared plus b x plus c, the Galois group is either trivial, if there is one repeated root, or the two-element cyclic group Z two, if there are two distinct roots that swap.

For a cubic, the Galois group is either the three-element cyclic group C three or the full six-element symmetric group S three, determined by the discriminant. The Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory establishes a one-to-one correspondence between subgroups of the Galois group and intermediate field extensions between the base field and the splitting field. Larger subgroups correspond to smaller fields.

A polynomial is solvable by radicals if and only if its Galois group is solvable. A solvable group has a normal series where each quotient is abelian, or equivalently, its derived series reaches the trivial group. The symmetric group S n is solvable only for n less than or equal to four. This rigorously explains why the quintic polynomial and higher degrees have no general closed-form radical solutions.

Galois' original eighteen thirty-two manuscript on permutation groups and field extensions was largely unread for years. The theory only gained recognition after Liouville published it in eighteen forty-six, more than a decade after Galois' death in a duel at age twenty. The Galois group acts on the roots, encoding all algebraic relationships. Studying this symmetry group reveals whether and how solutions can be expressed using radicals. Modern Galois theory extends to infinite extensions, p-adic fields, and Galois cohomology, with deep applications to algebraic number theory and arithmetic geometry.
